channel.title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Maritime
channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] Cyberattack on Brazil’s Santos port authority knocks out access-control and port-coordination systems, forcing contingency procedures at Latin America’s busiest port
item.description: The Santos Port Authority (APS), the state company that runs Brazil’s largest port, lost its IT systems on the morning of 6 November, the same day a power cut hit its servers, and on 10 November confirmed a cyberattack. Platforms for physical access control, cargo handling and port-operations coordination were affected, and some services moved to email and manual checks while systems were restored, slowing some procedures. São Paulo’s port security commission raised the port’s protection level to 2 of 3 on 8 November. By 16 November the main internal systems were in final tests, with about 70% of affected backups reported recovered; ship movements and land access continued throughout. Brazil’s Federal Police are investigating; the attacker, entry route and any data theft are undisclosed. Editorial assessment: gate access and berth coordination need a drilled manual fallback that does not depend on port-authority IT. - The Rio Times (16 Nov 2026, status update citing the Santos Port Authority); Interlira Reports (17 Nov 2026); DatamarNews (10–11 Nov 2026, citing A Tribuna); CyberDelegate (17 Nov 2026, citing Folha de S.Paulo, CNN Brasil and Agência Brasil); Port Continuity Brief (15 Nov 2026) - Outage from 6 Nov 2026; protection level raised 8 Nov; attack confirmed 10 Nov; core systems in final tests 16 Nov 2026; investigation ongoing

item.title: [High] Maersk confirms data was stolen from a legacy system it inherited, as the WhiteArmor ransomware group demands $5 million
item.category: Incident — Data theft from a legacy IT system Maersk inherited through an acquisition; WhiteArmor ransomware group demands $5 million; no operational disruption
item.description: Maersk confirmed on 11 November that an attacker extracted data from one IT system it inherited through an acquisition, after the WhiteArmor ransomware group listed the company on its leak site on 7 November and demanded $5 million in bitcoin within 30 days. WhiteArmor claims about 100 GB from a logistics platform linked to LF Logistics, which Maersk bought in 2022, including about 30,000 driver records, plaintext passwords and mobile-device logs; those claims are unverified. Maersk says the incident is isolated to a local system, that its findings so far strongly suggest no sensitive data was disclosed, and that other Maersk systems and partner API and EDI connections show no impact. It has not said how or when the attacker got in. Editorial assessment: acquired platforms that were never fully integrated are a standing blind spot. - Maersk statement, 11 Nov 2026 (via BleepingComputer and SecurityWeek); BleepingComputer, 11 Nov 2026; SecurityWeek; Splash247 and Marine Insight - Leak-site listing 7 Nov 2026; Maersk confirmation 11 Nov 2026; ransom deadline about 7 Dec 2026; investigation ongoing

item.title: [High] Iran-linked hackers are turning to physical sabotage, US officials told the WSJ, including breached networks aboard two Texas-bound tankers
item.category: Incident (reported) — Officials cited by the WSJ link Iran-linked hackers to breached networks aboard two Texas-bound tankers; no formal US attribution; France seeks EU sanctions over refrigeration sabotage
item.description: The Wall Street Journal reported on 13 November, citing US and Israeli officials, that Iran-linked hackers have moved from espionage toward physical sabotage, including breaching networks aboard two energy tankers bound for Texas and locking operators out of control panels at small Midwest water stations. It gave no tanker names or dates. The Coast Guard and FBI boarded two Texas-bound tankers in August, the Coast Guard confirmed a malicious cyber actor aboard one, VL Prosperity, and US officials said in September they were investigating possible Iranian involvement; no agency has formally attributed the incidents. In Europe, France blames Iran’s IRGC for October’s sabotage of supermarket refrigeration controllers and expects EU sanctions on 14 December; Iran denies involvement. Editorial assessment: vessel operators should plan for a state actor willing to tamper with shipboard systems. - Wall Street Journal, 13 Nov 2026 (via Newsmax wire on Yahoo News); Asharq Al-Awsat, 16 Nov 2026 (EU sanctions push); APA, 18 Nov 2026 (Barrot on France 5); Coast Guard and FBI statements (Sep 2026, via CBS News and gCaptain) - Tanker boardings 21 & 24 Aug 2026; WSJ report 13 Nov 2026; EU sanctions decision expected 14 Dec 2026

item.title: [High] CISA and FBI warn of an ongoing threat to internet-connected refrigeration as European supermarket attacks reach at least 11 countries
item.category: Incident — CISA/FBI/HHS/USDA/DOT joint warning (5 Nov 2026) and a second wave of refrigeration attacks across about 11 European countries (1–4 Nov); Belgium says its evidence points to Iran (12 Nov), no formal attribution
item.description: Hackers are tampering with internet-connected refrigeration controllers, and on 5 November CISA and the FBI, with HHS, USDA and DOT, warned the threat is ongoing and also reaches healthcare, chemical, transport and cold-storage operations. Hundreds of French supermarkets were hit in October; a second wave on 1–2 November reached about 11 European countries, forcing units into continuous heating or defrost. Sweden’s NCSC says victims mainly ran older systems from one manufacturer with weak passwords, and Sekoia says the second wave used a non-public, unauthenticated flaw that renames the controller’s admin account. Belgium says its evidence points to Iran, short of formal attribution (see the Iran card above). No port or vessel victim is reported. Editorial assessment: reefer yards and port cold stores with web-managed controllers should treat any internet-reachable unit as at risk. - TechCrunch (5 Nov 2026, CISA/FBI joint statement); SentinelOne Labs (3 Nov 2026, updated 4 Nov); Cybersecurity Dive (3 Nov 2026, updated with 4 Nov developments); Unit 42 (6 Nov 2026, exposure counts); Censys (6 Nov 2026, exposure analysis); BleepingComputer (5 Nov 2026); Nextgov (29 Oct 2026); Al Jazeera (4 Nov 2026); CERT-FR CERTFR-2026-ALE-012; The Cyber Express (6 Nov 2026, CISA/FBI/HHS/USDA/DOT advisory summary); Industrial Cyber (6 Nov 2026); Help Net Security (6 Nov 2026); SecurityWeek (6 Nov 2026, hardening guidance); The Hacker News (9 Nov 2026, exposure trend); eBuilder Security (11 Nov 2026, Swedish government and NCSC warning); Arab News/AFP (12 Nov 2026, Belgian statement); Sekoia TDR (10 Nov 2026, second-wave technique) - Attacks overnight 1–2 Nov 2026; Germany, Romania and UK confirmed 4 Nov 2026; CISA/FBI joint warning 5 Nov 2026; French attribution of the October attack 9 Nov 2026; Swedish government warning 10 Nov 2026; Belgian minister points to Iran 12 Nov 2026 — investigations ongoing

item.title: [Medium] Equinor says the cyberattack on its IT systems has been stopped after three days, as a second Norwegian energy firm reports an attempted attack
item.category: Incident — Cyberattack on certain IT systems at Norway’s Equinor, disclosed 17 Nov 2026 and declared stopped on 20 Nov 2026; production unaffected throughout; Skagerak Energi reported an attempted attack on 18 Nov 2026; no attribution
item.description: Equinor, Norway’s state-controlled energy company and the EU’s largest pipeline-gas supplier, said on 20 November that the cyberattack on certain IT systems it disclosed on 17 November has been stopped. Production ran normally throughout, and it has found no sign that data was stolen or altered. Equinor says the attack was not a self-spreading virus and did not appear aimed specifically at it; police and Norway’s National Security Authority, which raised the national cyber risk level to “high” on 27 October, are involved. A day after Equinor’s first report, utility Skagerak Energi reported an attempted attack with operations unaffected. Neither has disclosed the entry route or attacker, and nothing points to OT. For gas and crude export terminals, two incidents at Norwegian energy firms in one week are reason to check IT-to-OT boundaries now (editorial assessment). - Rigzone (20 Nov 2026, attack stopped; Skagerak Energi attempted attack); Riviera Maritime Media (20 Nov 2026, timeline of Equinor updates and NSM risk level); Equinor statements (17–20 Nov 2026); Reuters (19 Nov 2026, attack still ongoing); The Record (18 Nov 2026) - Disclosed 17 Nov 2026; declared stopped 20 Nov 2026; Skagerak attempt reported 18–19 Nov 2026

item.title: [Medium] n0n published data it says came from 38 port, shipping and logistics firms; none has confirmed a breach, and a shared software vendor is suspected
item.category: Incident (claimed) — Extortion group published data it says it took from 38 port, shipping and logistics firms; no victim has confirmed a breach
item.description: The data-theft extortion group n0n listed 38 maritime and logistics organizations in 18 countries on 12 October, including Ocean Network Express, Santos Brasil, TTI Algeciras and Eurogate Tanger, and claims EDI messages, manifests, vessel schedules, gate movements and terminal configuration records. SOCRadar and The Register reported on 28 and 30 October that all listings were published after the 19 October deadline, with no payments seen; the contents have not been independently analysed and no listed firm has confirmed a breach. Researchers link at least 21 of the 38 to customers of the South Korean maritime software provider CyberLogitec, which has not confirmed an incident; the link is unverified. SOCRadar found that the break-ins it could document relied on weak or stolen credentials, not exploits. No operational disruption is reported. - SOCRadar, 13 and 28 Oct 2026; The Register, 30 Oct 2026; SAFETY4SEA and Cydome, 14 Oct 2026; The Loadstar and MundoMaritimo - Batch posted 12 Oct 2026; deadline 19 Oct passed; listings reported published by 28 Oct; claims unverified

item.title: [High] China’s Volt Typhoon used throwaway relay chains to reach management and SD-WAN platforms at critical-infrastructure targets, maritime among them, Lumen says
item.category: Research — Lumen Black Lotus Labs on Volt Typhoon’s “Silent Train” relay framework; maritime among victim sectors; no OT access described
item.description: Lumen’s Black Lotus Labs reported on 28 October on “Silent Train”, the covert access framework it says the China state-sponsored group Volt Typhoon has used since November 2023: each session runs through a short-lived chain of compromised home-office routers, IoT devices and enterprise equipment, built for one target and then discarded. Lumen says the aim is to gain and keep access to management and control-plane technology, and cites zero-day campaigns against N-able N-central (CVE-2025-8875, CVE-2025-8876), Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN (CVE-2026-20127) and VeloCloud Orchestrator (CVE-2026-16812), all in CISA’s KEV catalog. It lists maritime among the critical-infrastructure sectors with victims but names none, gives no count by sector and describes no OT access or operational impact. Editorial assessment: in port and ship-management networks, the SD-WAN orchestrator or remote-management server that can reconfigure every site deserves the same protection as the OT behind it. - Lumen Black Lotus Labs, 28 Oct 2026 (primary); CyberScoop, 28 Oct 2026; KEV dates from CISA KEV via CIRCL - Activity since Nov 2023; report published 28 Oct 2026

item.title: [Medium] DHS tells Congress Iran-backed hackers have stepped up attacks on US water, energy and transport since February, while officials rule out hacking in last week’s outages
item.category: Government threat assessment — DHS Secretary’s written testimony to the House Homeland Security Committee (18 Nov 2026); DNI and DHS tell the same hearing recent US outages were not cyberattacks
item.description: In written testimony for a House Homeland Security Committee hearing on 18 November, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Iranian state-sponsored groups and pro-Iranian criminals have targeted US critical infrastructure since the conflict with Iran began in February, with transportation, healthcare, water, energy and financial services increasingly in their sights. He described the attacks so far as mostly localized, low-damage disruptions of poorly secured industrial control systems, but warned that weak systems and poor cyber hygiene could have devastating consequences. At the same hearing the Director of National Intelligence and DHS said they found no evidence that hackers caused last week’s Microsoft 365 outage, the nationwide FAA ground stop or other recent disruptions, which officials tie to software defects and upgrade failures. Separately, AttackIQ research released on 17 November describes Iranian groups handing network access to one another, with long-running espionage access later passed to teams pursuing destructive goals, sometimes disguised as ransomware or hacktivism, often reaching targets through contractors and suppliers. For port and vessel operators, the official US view now matches France’s: Iran is going after the weakest exposed controllers (editorial assessment). - Jerusalem Post (18 Nov 2026, Mullin written testimony); Report.az (18 Nov 2026); Bloomberg (18 Nov 2026); Federal News Network (18 Nov 2026, outages not a coordinated attack); Washington Examiner (18 Nov 2026, hearing); AttackIQ “Weighing Cyber Power”, via Water Online (17 Nov 2026) - Testimony and hearing 18 Nov 2026; AttackIQ research 17 Nov 2026

item.title: [Medium] Dragos counts 1,266 ransomware attacks on industrial organizations in Q3, up 11%, and found no case of an operator touching a control system
item.category: Research — Dragos Industrial Ransomware Analysis for Q3 2026 (published 16 Nov 2026), covering July–September; Check Point October 2026 statistics (12 Nov 2026) for comparison
item.description: Dragos said on 16 November that ransomware hit 1,266 industrial organizations between July and September 2026, up 11% on the second quarter, while the number of brands claiming industrial victims jumped from 70 to 99. Manufacturing took 69% of cases, followed by the ICS ecosystem of integrators, engineering firms and equipment makers (116) and transport and logistics (105); oil and gas logged 47. Qilin and The Gentlemen drove 29% of the total. Dragos saw no Q3 case of a ransomware operator manipulating a control system: production stopped because the IT, ERP and virtualization layers plants rely on went down, as when Fairlife reportedly halted all four of its US plants for about 11 days. Entry came through edge devices and enterprise applications exploited within days of disclosure, and through stolen VPN and firewall credentials. Check Point separately counted a record 1,063 claimed victims across all sectors in October. Dragos does not break out maritime; for carriers and terminals the lesson is the same IT-layer dependency (editorial assessment). - Dragos (16 Nov 2026); Australian Cyber Security Magazine (17 Nov 2026); Check Point Research October 2026 statistics, via iTWire (12 Nov 2026) - Published 16 Nov 2026; data covers July–September 2026

item.title: [Critical] Attackers rooted unpatched Check Point gateways through PHP2Shell, planted backdoors and wiped a VMware host; the root flaw is now in KEV
item.category: Incident — PHP2Shell plus Gaia root flaw CVE-2026-123039 used to backdoor Check Point gateways and wipe a VMware ESXi host (wave 1 from 30 Oct, Israel; wave 2 from 2 Nov, multiple countries); CVE-2026-123039 added to CISA KEV 13 Nov 2026
item.description: Check Point Research said on 12 November that attackers exploited the PHP2Shell flaws on unpatched Check Point Mobile Access portals from 30 October, then used a local flaw (CVE-2026-123039) to become root. They planted backdoors, pivoted to a VMware ESXi host and ran a wiper. The first wave hit Israeli organizations, some destructively; a second wave from 2 November reached several countries without destruction. Attribution is unconfirmed (tooling resembles China-nexus UNC5221). CISA added the root flaw to KEV on 13 November. No OT or maritime victim is reported, but such gateways often front port, terminal and fleet-management networks, and ESXi often hosts terminal-operating and monitoring servers (editorial assessment). - Check Point Research (12 Nov 2026); SecurityWeek (13 Nov 2026); Canadian Centre for Cyber Security AV26-1154 (12 Nov 2026, updated 13 Nov); CISA KEV alert (13 Nov 2026); BleepingComputer (Nov 2026) - Wave 1 from 30 Oct 2026; wave 2 from 2 Nov 2026; research published 12 Nov 2026; KEV addition 13 Nov 2026

item.title: [Critical] PHP2Shell attacks rooted about two dozen Palo Alto firewalls, and Siemens, Schneider and ABB now list grid-control, DCS and RTU products, several with no fix
item.category: Active exploitation — PHP2Shell chained with a Linux kernel flaw to root exposed PAN-OS firewalls, 23–24 Oct; OT vendor advisories 28–30 Oct; Siemens adds metering gateways 16 Nov
item.description: Palo Alto’s Unit 42 verified that a suspected China-nexus actor chained the PHP2Shell flaws (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619) with Linux kernel bug CVE-2026-46300 to root about two dozen internet-exposed PAN-OS firewalls on 23–24 October and steal Active Directory credentials. Siemens (Spectrum Power, AMIS TS and, since 16 November, WTV676/WTV776 metering gateways), Schneider (a Foxboro DCS server) and ABB (Netcontrol RTUs, ASPECT gateways) now list affected products, several unfixed. None is reported exploited and no OT or maritime operator is named: treat it as an IT-to-OT boundary warning for port and terminal networks (editorial assessment). - Unit 42 (updated 29 Oct 2026); Palo Alto Networks advisory for CVE-2026-109618 (updated 29 Oct 2026); The Record (29 Oct 2026) and Infosecurity Magazine (30 Oct 2026), citing Dream; CISA KEV catalog (30 Oct 2026 release); Siemens SSA-166980 V1.4 (16 Nov 2026, WTV676/WTV776 added; V1.2 29 Oct 2026), SSA-566512 V1.1 (28 Oct 2026), SSA-019113 and SSA-082556; Schneider Electric SESB-2026-295-01 v3.2.0 (30 Oct 2026); ABB Netcontrol and Arctic advisories (30 Oct 2026), ASPECT advisory (29 Oct 2026) and APROL SA26P015 (23 Oct 2026); CERT@VDE VDE-2026-127 and VDE-2026-137 - Root compromises 23–24 Oct 2026, verified by Unit 42 29 Oct 2026; KEV additions 26 and 28 Oct 2026; Siemens, Schneider and ABB updates 28–30 Oct 2026; Siemens metering gateways added 16 Nov 2026

item.title: [High] A vCenter authentication bypass was exploited as a zero-day for two months before Broadcom’s 19 November patch; vCenter 7.0 gets no fix
item.category: Active exploitation — VMware vCenter authentication bypass CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS 9.8) exploited as a zero-day for more than two months by a suspected China-linked group, per Mandiant; Broadcom fix released 19 Nov 2026; no public fix for vCenter 7.0
item.description: Broadcom patched CVE-2026-123890 on 19 November, a critical flaw in vCenter’s directory service that lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker obtain an administrator session. Google’s Mandiant, which reported the bug, says a suspected China-linked espionage group it tracks as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221, also called Warp Panda) exploited it for more than two months beforehand. In the incidents Mandiant investigated, the group got in through a BeyondTrust Remote Support flaw, moved to Linux appliances, attacked vCenter in early September with a custom tool called Bonesaw, stole SAML signing material and the vCenter master key, created an SSO admin account, forged tokens and moved on to ESXi hosts. Fixes are in vCenter 9.1.1.0200, 9.0.2.0200 and 8.0 U3m; end-of-life vCenter 7.0 has no public patch. No victims or sectors are named. Terminal operating systems, port-community servers and OT monitoring tools often run as virtual machines, so whoever controls vCenter controls those hosts (editorial assessment). - SecurityWeek (19 Nov 2026, citing Broadcom, Google Threat Intelligence/Mandiant and Mandiant CTO Charles Carmakal); CISA KEV alert (20 Nov 2026); The Hacker News (20–21 Nov 2026) - Added to CISA KEV 20 Nov 2026; patched 19 Nov 2026; exploited from at least early Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Attackers root clustered Cisco Expressway gateways soon after a public exploit, and CISA adds the flaw to KEV
item.category: Active exploitation — Cisco Expressway CVE-2026-76466 (CVSS 9.8), clustered Expressway Core/Edge; exploited after a public PoC (reported by F6); added to CISA KEV 20 Nov 2026; fixed in X15.5.20
item.description: Security firm F6 says attackers exploited CVE-2026-76466, a critical flaw in clustered Cisco Expressway Core and Edge deployments, shortly after proof-of-concept code appeared on GitHub. They broke into two internet-facing Expressway nodes at an unnamed Russian organization, moved to two more cluster nodes inside the network, and gained root. From there they ran Python scripts, which F6 says show signs of AI-assisted writing, to scan for SMB shares, SQL Server and WinRM hosts and to search GitLab for credentials. CISA added the flaw to its KEV catalog on 20 November alongside the vCenter zero-day. Cisco disclosed and fixed it on 21 October; there is no workaround. No OT victim is reported, but Expressway is a perimeter gateway that often bridges outside callers into internal networks, so an exposed, unpatched cluster is a foothold close to terminal and port-operations systems (editorial assessment). - Security Affairs (21 Nov 2026, CISA KEV additions of 20 Nov); SecurityWeek (Nov 2026, citing F6); Security Affairs (20 Nov 2026, F6 findings) - Added to CISA KEV 20 Nov 2026; exploitation reported 18–20 Nov 2026; patched 21 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] N-able ships Hotfix 3 for 17 more N-central flaws after attackers planted miners on servers already running Hotfix 2
item.category: Active exploitation — N-able N-central: 4EverAble2Shell exploited to plant miners (13 Nov 2026); N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 3 fixes 17 more CVEs and removes the Legacy API (16–17 Nov 2026); separate breach of N-able’s hosted Mail Assure/SpamExperts cloud disclosed 20 Nov 2026
item.description: N-able released N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 3 on 16 November, which it calls a critical security update. It fixes 17 new CVEs, including authentication bypasses, missing authorization checks, path traversal leading to code execution and a syslog injection that runs commands as root, and it removes the Legacy API option that the actively exploited 4EverAble2Shell chain depends on. On-premises servers need the upgrade now; hosted servers update automatically, but every customer must also upgrade Agents and Probes, which N-able warns can otherwise be impersonated. The fix follows Huntback’s 13 November finding of cryptocurrency miners on 21 N-central servers, 19 of them on Hotfix 2. Remote control and Intune integration stay blocked for now. Separately, N-able said on 20 November that attackers reached a server in its hosted Mail Assure and SpamExperts email-filtering cloud, forcing it to take the management portal and APIs offline; it says mail flow continued, it has found no access to customer data, and the breach is unrelated to N-central. Many managed-service providers run port, terminal and ship-management Windows hosts through RMM tools, and a miner today can be a hands-on intruder tomorrow (editorial assessment). - BleepingComputer (20 Nov 2026, Mail Assure/SpamExperts breach); The Hacker News (17 Nov 2026, Hotfix 3, citing N-able release notes of 16 Nov); The Hacker News (13 Nov 2026, citing Huntback and Previdian); The Hacker News (12 Nov 2026, new chains); SecurityWeek (13 Nov 2026); Tenable (10 Nov 2026) - Mail Assure breach disclosed 20 Nov 2026; Hotfix 3 released 16 Nov 2026; exploitation reported 13 Nov 2026; Able2Shell disclosed 9 Nov 2026

item.title: [High] Java4Shell exploitation attempts begin, and Siemens tells customers to take Industrial Edge Management offline until patched
item.category: Advisory — OpenJDK “Java4Shell” memory-corruption flaw CVE-2026-114938 (disclosed and patched 17 Nov 2026); exploitation attempts seen 18–19 Nov 2026; Siemens SSA-272816 lists three Industrial Edge Management products
item.description: Probing for Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a memory-corruption bug in how OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later decode Base64 data, started within two days of its 17 November disclosure. GreyNoise counted more than 150 matching requests from five addresses by early 19 November and Previdian logged nine attempts from six addresses; none is confirmed to have succeeded. Exploitation needs a recent Intel or AMD x86-64 processor with AVX-512 VBMI, and researchers at Calif showed unauthenticated code execution against default Jira, Confluence, Jenkins and Keycloak setups, each with a tailored chain. For OT teams the key item is Siemens advisory SSA-272816: three Industrial Edge Management products are affected, fixes are in progress, and Siemens recommends taking those instances offline until they are patched. Cisco lists more than a dozen products with no fix yet, and Atlassian Data Center products are also unpatched. - SecurityWeek (19 Nov 2026, citing Calif, GreyNoise, WatchTowr, Cloudflare, Previdian, Siemens SSA-272816, Cisco and Atlassian); The Record (18 Nov 2026, CISA alert) - Disclosed and patched 17 Nov 2026; exploitation attempts 18–19 Nov 2026

item.title: [Medium] Moxa: its Remote Connect client could be fooled by a fake server, and the end-of-life OnCell G3150A-LTE cellular gateway will get no fix
item.category: Advisory — Remote-access client and wireless device server fixed; end-of-life cellular gateway left unfixed
item.description: Moxa published advisory MPSA-269510 on 27 October covering two products used to reach remote field equipment. CVE-2026-111459 (CVSS v4.0 7.6, scored by Moxa) is an improper certificate-validation flaw in the Moxa Remote Connect Suite client (MRC Client) 1.0.0 through 4.2.0: an attacker positioned between the client and its server could impersonate the server, which supplies the client’s OpenVPN configuration, and read or alter the traffic. Version 4.2.2 fixes it and is obtained through Moxa technical support. The OnCell G3150A-LTE cellular gateway has static HTTPS and CA private keys in its firmware (CVE-2026-111460, v4.0 7.7) and an OS command injection reachable through SMS management by an attacker with high privileges (CVE-2026-111461, v4.0 7.5). Moxa considers the gateway end-of-life and will not fix it; the mitigations are resetting the device to regenerate its keys and keeping SMS management disabled, which is the default. In a second advisory the same day, MPSA-261250, Moxa covers CVE-2026-111548 (v4.0 5.3, scored by Moxa), which lets an authenticated attacker crash the web management interface of NPort W2150A-W4 and W2250A-W4 wireless device servers until they are power-cycled; their other functions keep running, and the fix comes through Moxa support (CERT-FR lists firmware 1.5.9). No exploitation of any of these flaws has been reported. Editorial assessment: remote-connect clients and cellular gateways like these link remote port-side equipment and terminal sites back to engineers and vendors, so unsupported units should be retired rather than left in place. - Moxa MPSA-269510 and MPSA-261250, 27 Oct 2026 (primary); CVE records (Moxa as CNA) via CIRCL; CERT-FR CERTFR-2026-AVI-1393 - Published 27 Oct 2026; MRC Client fixed in 4.2.2; OnCell G3150A-LTE end-of-life

item.title: [Info] ClassNK publishes the second edition of its ship cyber security management guidelines, with audit criteria mapped to RightShip, SIRE 2.0, DryBMS and TMSA vetting
item.category: Guidance — Classification-society guidelines for ship cyber security management systems (voluntary certification); no CVE
item.description: Classification society ClassNK announced on 30 October the second edition of its guidelines for cyber security management systems (CSMS) on ships and clarified its certification requirements, Maritime Gateway reported on 3 November. The guidelines now come in two parts: Part 1 sets out the CSMS requirements and Part 2 the audit criteria and the evidence auditors expect. The structure references ISO/IEC 27001 and 27002 and covers management commitment, shore and onboard responsibilities, risk assessment, operational controls and incident preparedness, and the audit criteria are mapped to the RightShip (RISQ), OCIMF SIRE 2.0, DryBMS and TMSA vetting schemes. The guidelines are available through ClassNK’s My Page portal after registration, and are separate from IACS unified requirements E26 and E27, which apply to ships contracted for construction on or after 1 July 2024. Editorial assessment: tanker and bulk operators facing several vetting regimes can build one evidence set for all of them. - Maritime Gateway, 3 Nov 2026 (citing ClassNK’s 30 Oct announcement); MarineLink, 30 Oct 2026 - Second edition announced 30 Oct 2026

item.title: [Info] Class societies, maritime security vendors and MTS-ISAC launch the Maritime Vulnerabilities Repository for ship and port IT/OT flaws
item.category: Industry initiative — Maritime vulnerability database from security vendors, class societies and an ISAC
item.description: A coalition calling itself the Blue Initiative, made up of Cydome, Rakuten Maritime, the classification societies Bureau Veritas and ClassNK, and the Maritime Transportation System ISAC (MTS-ISAC), launched the Maritime Vulnerabilities Repository on or before 26 October, Infosecurity Magazine reported that day. It is billed as the first database to list only IT and OT vulnerabilities relevant to the maritime sector. Researchers from Cydome and the other partners validate proposed entries before publication, and Infosecurity says vulnerabilities are published only once a patch is available. Users can browse CVEs, filter by equipment or vendor, read expert analysis and subscribe to alerts. Cydome’s chief executive describes the aim as a “public and open single source of truth” for maritime vulnerabilities. SecurityWeek, which describes the database as free, also reports entry counts that could not be verified independently, so they are left out here. It is a resource, not a new threat. Editorial assessment: it gives ship managers and terminal operators a maritime-specific list to check assets against, but because it waits for a patch, vendor PSIRTs and CISA ICS advisories remain the place to learn about unfixed flaws. - Infosecurity Magazine, 26 Oct 2026 (launch report; no partner press release found); SecurityWeek, 27 Oct 2026; Splash - Launched on or before 26 Oct 2026
